doc.title: Pete Levin interviewed by Monk Rowe, Danbury, Connecticut, November 20, 2001

title: Working with Paul Simon, Annie Lennox and Peter Gabriel
summary: Levin compares pop artists: Paul Simon, Annie Lennox's scripted approach, and Peter Gabriel's looseness on tour.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans
story.community_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans

blocks.x: Of the pop people that you’ve worked with, do any of them stand out as particularly memorable? Enjoyable?

Oh sure. They’re all enjoyable — Paul Simon is one of my favorite composers. That says a lot. Just to be on stage with him and doing his music is great. Annie Lennox who I did more recently, Annie is a wonderful singer and I like her music a lot. Performing it is a restricted situation. Annie works out carefully what it is she wants to do and she is very good at that so the performance — here’s the record—

We’re duplicating that and we’re going to re-create it live and don’t stray at all. That’s it. I’m not being critical of that, I mean it’s a very viable situation, certainly as a performance it makes a great performance. I always thought Annie had it in her, I get a very bluesy feeling from her singing. I think that’s inside of her. I think she could probably stretch out and improvise a lot and definitely hold her own. I mean she’s a tremendous talent and she’s got a great voice. But she feels it’s important to work out how she’s going to do something and then do that, and she doesn’t want to stray from it so of course it’s important for her to have — you don’t want a bunch of jazz guys in back — let’s try this, I’ve got a great groove for this. No. That doesn’t work.
Almost more like an actress would. More like scripted. Want to stick to the script.

A little bit. Yeah that is it. If we could qualify it and make it a stage actress as opposed to film. Because things can change. I mean it’s never absolutely pat in the same way, otherwise why go to a concert, you’d better listen to the record. But to work out a show and know what’s going to happen, just work out the strongest way of putting the music across. That’s more important for a pop artist I think than a jazz artist. A jazz artist

everybody knows is going to be different every time so it’s okay. I think somebody like Annie, where the fans really want to hear the song the way they just heard it on the record. Some of them would like it if it strays a little bit, a lot wouldn’t. Peter Gabriel was also a tremendous artist and a very creative thinker. I always respected him for going out on live tours, big tours supporting major albums, and he would just go with his band. And they would kind of do the same arrangements but they didn’t sound exactly the same. Yet he was confident enough to allow that leeway, which I think takes a lot. It’s a lot of pressure on you, playing to fifteen thousand people, that’s a lot of pressure, and you’re judged by everything, every time you open your mouth.
